## How Animals Sense Their World {background-color="#1B4332"}

## The senses animals have

- Vision, hearing/vibration, touch, taste, **smell** — most animals
  combine several
- Chemical senses (taste + smell) are the **oldest and most universal**:
  even single-celled organisms and bacteria sense and respond to
  chemicals (e.g. quorum sensing)
- Insects lean heavily on smell: **antennae** (primary olfactory organ)

::: {.notes}

animal kingdom is chemically-dominant. Callback opportunity to Story 1

## Why chemical communication? {.hook}

> **Why might a species evolve to "talk" with chemicals instead of
> sound or light?**
>
> *Pourquoi une espèce évoluerait-elle pour « parler » avec des
> produits chimiques plutôt qu'avec du son ou de la lumière ?*


::: {.notes}
Let a few guesses land. Push toward: works in total darkness, doesn't
need line-of-sight, travels around obstacles, can persist after the
sender has left (a trail, a mark), can be extremely specific (exact
blend and ratio), cheap to produce compared to sound/light displays.
~2 min including the reveal below.
:::

## Chemical communication: 

- Ancient and ubiquitous
- Functional in the dark, underground, or underwater
- Flexible in distance (compare to gustatory and visual signals)
- Can **persist** after the sender is gone (a scent mark, a trail)
- Extremely specific and diverse: <br>
    - exact compound + ratio + concentration <br>
    - small modification will turn one compound to another 


## Specificity 
![](images/Reprisolation.png)

::: {.notes}
The two species studied are Adoxophyes orana (summer fruit tortrix) and Clepsis spectrana (carnation tortrix), two tortricid moths that are sympatric across much of Europe. The central question: how do the males of each species find the right female, given that they live in the same habitat?

Males of each species responded strongly only to their own species' blend ratio. Adoxophyes orana males were attracted to Z9-dominant blends; Clepsis spectrana males to Z11-dominant blends. The other species' ratio was unattractive, and in some cases inhibitory. Two species, two pheromone systems, same two molecules.

Minks et al. showed that ratio alone — not molecular identity — is sufficient to maintain complete reproductive isolation between two sympatric species.
:::
